idiom_name: optional capability interface discovered with a comma-ok type assertion (io.WriterTo, http.Flusher)
implementation_notes: Go interfaces are satisfied implicitly, so a client can declare exactly the capability it needs and any existing type that has the method already implements it - the base interface never changes and no implementor is touched, which is the pattern's preservation guarantee for free. The lookup is the comma-ok type assertion on an interface value, the form the standard library uses to keep io and net/http small: if wt, ok := src.(io.WriterTo); ok { wt.WriteTo(dst) }, with io.ReaderFrom/WriterTo, http.Flusher/Hijacker/Pusher, fmt.Stringer and io.Closer as the canonical optional interfaces; the single-return form v.(T) panics and therefore never qualifies as a total query. Supplying an extension for a type that does not have the method is deliberately awkward - method sets are fixed at compile time and an embedding wrapper erases the optional interfaces it does not re-expose - so the community advice is to treat optional interfaces as a compatibility or optimisation device, not as a general extension mechanism, and to put capabilities the caller requires into the function signature.
pitfalls: The single-return assertion v.(T) panics when the capability is absent; a negotiation point always uses the comma-ok form.

Wrapping a value in a struct that embeds only the base interface erases its optional interfaces at compile time: the capability silently disappears and only runtime tests notice (the http.Flusher middleware trap).
Implementing the method is not the same as supporting it - io.Seeker-style capabilities can be present but fail on use, so callers still need a fallback path.
A capability the caller needs for correctness (hijacking a connection) cannot be made optional by type assertion; it becomes a runtime error path, so pass it in the signature instead.
